chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Building Blocks of a DCF

lessons.title: WACC Explained with an Indian Listed Company

children.text: A DCF built on free cash flow to the firm needs one discount rate for cash that belongs to two very different groups: lenders, who are paid first and accept a lower return, and shareholders, who are paid last and demand more. The weighted average cost of capital blends the two. It looks like a simple average, and that is exactly why it is so often done wrong. This lesson builds WACC for Kaveri Ridge Cement from the ground up, using the same sources you would use for any NSE-listed company.

body.text: WACC is the minimum return a business must earn on all of its capital to keep both lenders and shareholders satisfied. Weight each source at market value, use the cost of debt after tax, and keep every input consistent with the cash flows you are discounting.

body.caption: E = market value of equity, D = value of debt, Ke = cost of equity, Kd = pre-tax cost of debt, t = marginal tax rate

children.text: Four inputs, four steps. Kaveri Ridge Cement Ltd is the fictional NSE-listed cement maker from the last two lessons.
Step 1: Market Value of Equity and Debt
Weights must reflect what each claim is worth today, not what was originally invested. For equity, that is simply
market capitalisation

. For debt, Indian companies mostly borrow through bank term loans and unlisted or thinly traded NCDs, so the book value of borrowings is a reasonable stand-in for market value unless interest rates or the company's credit quality have changed sharply.

markDefs.definition: Share price multiplied by total shares outstanding. The market value of a company's equity.

body.caption: Kaveri Ridge Cement: capital structure at market value (₹ crore, illustrative)

body.text: Use net debt or gross debt, but be consistent. If you weight WACC using net debt, subtract net debt when you move from enterprise value to equity value. Using gross debt in one place and net debt in the other quietly misstates the answer. Lease liabilities under Ind AS 116 follow the same rule: if you treat them as debt in the weights, treat lease payments as financing in your cash flows and subtract lease liabilities in the equity bridge.

children.text: Step 2: Cost of Equity

From the last lesson: an unlevered cement beta of 0.75, relevered at Kaveri Ridge's debt-to-equity ratio of 0.20 (₹1,500 ÷ ₹7,500 crore), gives a levered beta of 0.86. With a 6.5% risk-free rate and a 7.0% ERP:

body.label: Kaveri Ridge cost of equity
body.context: 6.5% + 0.86 × 7.0%. Always relever beta using the same market-value weights you use in WACC.

children.text: Step 3: Pre-Tax Cost of Debt
The cost of debt in WACC is what the company would pay to borrow today, not what it paid years ago. There are three ways to estimate it, from best to weakest.

body.caption: Estimating the pre-tax cost of debt for an Indian company

cells: 1. Market yield on the company's own bonds
Current yield on its listed NCDs or bonds, from NSE, BSE or the debt segment
Best, when the bonds trade actively. Many Indian issues rarely trade.
Take the long-term rating from CRISIL, ICRA, CARE or India Ratings, then add a typical spread for that rating to the G-sec yield
The most practical route for most listed companies
Interest cost from the P&L divided by average borrowings
Only as a cross-check. It reflects old borrowing costs, subsidised loans and past ratings.

body.caption: Illustrative spreads over the 10-year G-sec by long-term rating
headers: Implied pre-tax Kd at a 6.5% G-sec

cells: 5% and above, often unavailable from banks

body.label: CRISIL Ratings
body.description: Search a company to read its rating rationale, which covers debt levels, liquidity, key risks and rating history. ICRA, CARE Ratings and India Ratings publish similar rationales on their own websites.

children.text: Kaveri Ridge's term loans carry a (fictional) long-term rating of A+. Using a 2.0% spread over the 6.5% G-sec yield gives a pre-tax cost of debt of 8.5%. Its P&L shows interest of ₹120 crore on ₹1,500 crore of net debt, a historical rate of only 8.0%, because part of its debt was raised when rates were lower. For valuation, use 8.5%.
Step 4: The Tax Shield
Interest is deductible for tax, so every ₹100 of interest reduces the tax bill. This
interest tax shield
makes debt cheaper than its headline rate.

markDefs.definition: The reduction in tax payable because interest expense is deductible. It lowers the effective cost of debt to Kd × (1 - t).

body.text: Use the marginal tax rate the company will actually save on its next rupee of interest, not a blended effective rate from the P&L. We use 25% for consistency with earlier lessons; companies under India's concessional corporate tax regime pay about 25.17% including surcharge and cess. A company with large carried-forward losses or tax-exempt profits saves little or no tax on interest today, so its tax shield, and the benefit of its debt, is smaller than the formula assumes.

children.text: Putting It Together

body.caption: Kaveri Ridge Cement: WACC (components may not add exactly due to rounding)

body.label: Kaveri Ridge Cement WACC
body.context: The discount rate for its FCFF. Anything earning less than this on new projects destroys value for shareholders.

children.text: The Book-Value Trap

The most common WACC error in Indian research notes and student models is using book values instead of market values. Kaveri Ridge's balance sheet shows shareholders' equity of ₹4,000 crore, just over half its market value.

columns.label: Book-value weights (incorrect)
points: Enterprise value at 5% growth: ₹9,411 crore, 11% higher

children.text: Book values understate equity for any company trading above book, which is most of the Nifty. That overweights cheap debt, lowers WACC and inflates value. Here, with FCFF of ₹550 crore growing at 5% forever, the error adds about 11% to enterprise value, and even more to equity value once debt is subtracted.
Does More Debt Always Lower WACC?

Debt is cheaper than equity, so it is tempting to think more debt always lowers WACC. It does, but only up to a point. Each extra rupee of debt makes the remaining equity riskier, raising its beta, and eventually makes lenders charge more too.

body.title: Kaveri Ridge: WACC at different debt levels (illustrative)
Show me the numbers behind the chart

content.caption: Unlevered beta 0.75, Rf 6.5%, ERP 7.0%, tax 25%; cost of debt assumed to rise with leverage

children.text: In this illustration WACC falls from 11.75% with no debt to 11.46% at 20% debt, then rises again, reaching 12.91% at 60% debt. The model also leaves out the real costs of financial distress: lost customers, supplier credit being withdrawn, and management attention diverted to lenders. Indian investors saw these costs play out in heavily indebted power, infrastructure and telecom companies during the 2010s.

body.text: If a company is changing its capital structure, such as a promoter selling a stake to repay debt or a large debt-funded capex plan, use the target debt-to-capital ratio it will operate at, not today's. Management commentary, rating rationales and industry averages are useful guides to that target.

children.text: Check Your Understanding

body.title: Calculate WACC
body.prompt: A listed hospital chain is funded 80% by equity and 20% by debt at market values. Its cost of equity is 13%, its pre-tax cost of debt is 9% and its tax rate is 25%. What is its WACC, in %?

body.title: Why market values?
body.question: Why should WACC use the market value of equity rather than the book value from the balance sheet?
options: Because SEBI requires it in all valuation reports
Because book value is always higher than market value
Because investors require a return on what their claim is worth today, not on what was originally invested
Because market values make WACC lower
body.explanation: The cost of capital is an opportunity cost. A shareholder could sell at today's market price and invest elsewhere, so the return they require applies to the market value of their stake. For most Indian companies trading above book value, using book weights understates equity, lowers WACC and inflates value.

body.title: The tax shield
body.textWithBlank: Because interest is tax-deductible, the cost of debt used in WACC is the pre-tax rate multiplied by (1 - ___ rate).
body.explanation: The after-tax cost of debt is Kd × (1 - t), using the marginal tax rate the company actually saves on additional interest.

body.title: The 9% WACC that is too good to be true
body.scenario: Nikhil, a finance student in Pune, is valuing a mid-cap specialty chemicals company for a stock pitch. The company has ₹1,500 crore of debt and a market capitalisation of ₹6,000 crore, but its balance sheet shows shareholders' equity of only ₹1,500 crore. Its P&L shows interest of ₹75 crore, so Nikhil uses a 5% cost of debt. Last month, the company's rating was downgraded to BBB+ and its latest NCD issue was priced at 10.5%. Using a 14% cost of equity, book-value weights and a 5% pre-tax cost of debt, he calculates a WACC of 8.88%.
body.prompt: Identify the errors and recalculate WACC. The tax rate is 25%.
body.modelAnswer:
Error 1: Book-value weights. With book equity of ₹1,500 crore, Nikhil gives debt a 50% weight. At market value, equity is ₹6,000 crore, so the weights are 80.0% equity and 20.0% debt.

Error 2: A historical cost of debt. ₹75 crore of interest on ₹1,500 crore of debt reflects old, cheaper borrowing. The company would pay about 10.5% to borrow today, as its latest NCD issue shows.

Error 3: Ignoring the downgrade. A BBB+ rating confirms that lenders now see more risk. It is also a reason to check whether the 14% cost of equity reflects the higher leverage and risk.

Corrected WACC = 80.0% × 14% + 20.0% × 10.5% × (1 - 0.25) = 12.78%.

The errors understated WACC by about 3.9 percentage points. In a DCF with long-term growth of 5% to 6%, that gap would inflate the valuation dramatically, and the stock pitch would be built on the discount rate, not the business.

body.title: Build WACC for a company you own
steps: On screener.in, note the market capitalisation, total borrowings and cash and investments. Calculate net debt and the market-value weights.
Find the long-term rating in the latest rating rationale from CRISIL, ICRA, CARE or India Ratings, and estimate a spread over the current 10-year G-sec yield.
Cross-check with interest expense divided by average borrowings. If the two differ by a lot, find out why.
Estimate the cost of equity using a bottom-up beta relevered at the market-value debt-to-equity ratio.
Apply the marginal tax rate to the cost of debt and calculate WACC.
Sanity check: WACC should sit between the after-tax cost of debt and the cost of equity, and closer to the cost of equity for a lightly indebted company.

points: WACC blends the cost of equity and the after-tax cost of debt, weighted by their market values.
Use market capitalisation for equity. Book value of borrowings is usually an acceptable proxy for Indian corporate debt.
Estimate the cost of debt from current market yields or the credit rating plus a spread, not from historical interest expense.
Apply the marginal tax rate to the cost of debt, and reduce the tax shield for companies that are not paying tax.
Book-value weights overweight debt for companies trading above book, lowering WACC and inflating value.
More debt lowers WACC only up to a point. Beyond it, rising costs of equity and debt, and distress risk, push WACC back up.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Kaveri Ridge Cement Ltd, its rating and the individuals named are fictional, and all figures, including the rating spreads, are illustrative. Actual credit spreads vary with market conditions, issuer and tenure. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before making investment decisions.
